title: Middle Value of Two Sorted Lists
statement:
You get two lists a and b, each sorted ascending. Either one may be empty, but not both. Values may repeat.

Return the median of all a.length + b.length values taken together: the middle value if the total count is odd, or the average of the two middle values if it is even. Answers within 10⁻⁵ are accepted.

An O(m + n) merge is accepted by the tests. The real goal, and the one interviewers ask for, is O(log(min(m, n))).

examples.why: Together they are 3, 5, 8, 12, 20. Five values, so the third one, 8, is the median.
Together: 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11. Both middle values, 3 and 4, come from b. Taking each list's own median (10.5 and 2.5) and averaging gives 6.5, which is wrong.
One list is empty, so the answer is just the other list's median. The partition search must not read from the empty list.

hints: Merging the two lists and picking the middle is O(m + n). You only need the middle, so what part of the merge is wasted?
Cut a after i items and b after j items so that the two left parts together hold half of all values. Once you pick i, j is fixed. When is that cut the correct one?

The cut is correct when a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i] (treat missing items as −∞ / +∞). If a[i − 1] is too big, move i left; if b[j − 1] is too big, move i right. Binary search i over the shorter list.

explain.intuition:
The median splits all values into a left half and a right half where everything on the left is ≤ everything on the right. Any such split takes some prefix of a (say i items) and some prefix of b (j items), with i + j = half. So you are not searching for a value, you are searching for where to cut a; the cut in b follows from it.

Each list is sorted, so within a list the left part is already ≤ the right part. Only the cross pairs need checking: a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i]. If a[i − 1] > b[j], too much of a went left: move i left. If b[j − 1] > a[i], too little did: move i right. That is a monotone yes/no on i, so binary search it, over the shorter list so j never goes negative. Then the median is the largest value on the left (odd total), or that averaged with the smallest value on the right (even total).
steps: If a is longer than b, swap them. Let half = floor((m + n + 1) / 2); the left part gets the extra item when the total is odd.
Binary search i in [0, m] (inclusive, since taking none or all of a is allowed). Set j = half − i.
Read the four border values, using −∞ when i = 0 or j = 0 and +∞ when i = m or j = n: aLeft, aRight, bLeft, bRight.
If aLeft > bRight, set hi = i − 1. Else if bLeft > aRight, set lo = i + 1. Otherwise the cut is right.
At the right cut: odd total → max(aLeft, bLeft); even total → (max(aLeft, bLeft) + min(aRight, bRight)) / 2.
pitfalls: Using half = floor((m + n) / 2) and then returning max of the left side for odd totals. With that half the extra item lands on the right, so the median is min of the right side. Pick one convention and use it in both places.
Searching over the longer list. Then j = half − i can be negative or larger than n, and the border reads go out of range.
Searching i in [0, m − 1]. The correct cut can take all of a (i = m), as in a = [1, 2, 3], b = [7, 8, 9], so the inclusive upper bound is m, not m − 1.

solutions.title: Merge up to the middle
solutions.idea: Walk both lists with two pointers like a merge, but stop once you have passed the middle, remembering the last two values taken.

solutions.title: Binary search the cut in the shorter list
solutions.idea: Choose how many items of the shorter list go into the left half; the other list's count follows. Move the cut until the cross borders are in order.

followups: Generalise: return the k-th smallest value of the two lists in O(log k). How does discarding k/2 items at a time work?
The values arrive as a stream and you need the median after each one. Which two structures keep that cheap?
